items.reference: Let me explain how the conditioning work is supposed to land. WhisperKit accepts a promptTokens array inside DecodingOptions, and whatever we pass there becomes the previous context for the decoder. The catch is that the prompt is trimmed to half the token window, so we cannot just dump the whole session transcript into it. We keep the most recent sentences, cap the budget, and drop the prompt entirely whenever the previous decode looked suspicious. That last guard matters because a bad prompt can push the model into a repetition loop, and a repetition loop in a dictation app is far worse than a missing word.

items.reference: Thanks everyone for joining the retrospective. Overall the launch went smoothly, but there are three things we should do better next time. First, the support documentation went live two days after the feature, which left the help desk answering the same question over and over. Second, we never agreed on who owns the status page, so updates during the incident were slow. Third, and this is the big one, we shipped on a Friday. Nobody wants to debug a payment issue at nine in the evening before a weekend. Let's write these down and actually read them before the next release.

items.reference: Here is the incident summary for the outage on Tuesday. At around 2:15 pm the PostgreSQL primary ran out of connections because a batch job leaked them for over an hour. The Kubernetes autoscaler then made things worse by doubling the number of workers, each of which opened its own pool. Latency climbed past eight seconds and checkout effectively stopped. We recovered by killing the batch job and cycling the connection pooler, and the whole event lasted 34 minutes. The follow up items are a connection budget per service and an alert on pool saturation, both assigned and due next sprint.

items.reference: I want to dictate some thoughts about the book before I forget them. The first half is a fairly conventional memoir, childhood, school, the move to the city, but the voice is so dry and funny that none of it drags. Then the middle section switches to the mother's letters and the whole thing opens up. You suddenly understand that every story in the first half was secondhand, and the letters quietly correct the record. The ending felt rushed to me, maybe twenty pages where it needed sixty, but I still think it is the best thing she has written.

items.reference: Here is my honest review of the trip for the travel blog. The old town is genuinely beautiful, narrow streets, tiled courtyards, and the kind of bakeries that make you plan your day around bread. The catch is the crowds. By ten in the morning the main square is shoulder to shoulder, and the famous viewpoint has a queue like an airport. Go at sunrise or do not go at all. Food was cheaper than I expected, dinner for two came to about 40 euros with wine, and the seafood place by the harbor deserves every bit of its reputation.

If anything spikes we pull the appcast entry, which stops new updates without affecting anyone who already installed.

items.reference: Some notes for the garden this autumn. The tomatoes are done, pull them out and compost everything that is not diseased. The two plants with the curled leaves go in the bin, not the compost, just to be safe. Garlic goes in before the first frost, pointy end up, about a hand's width apart. Last year we planted too shallow and half of it heaved out of the ground by February. The roses get one last feed, then nothing until spring. And please label the beds this time, because by March nobody remembers what is where.

items.reference: Frontend migration update. We are about 70% of the way through converting the dashboard to TypeScript, and the strictness is already paying for itself. Last week the compiler caught a null flowing into the chart component that would have been a production crash. The npm workspace split also landed, so the design system builds independently and the main app no longer rebuilds the world on every change. Local build times dropped from four minutes to about 90 seconds. Remaining work is the settings pages and the test utilities, both scheduled for the next two sprints.

items.reference: Here is the local model setup I recommend for the polish stage. Install Ollama for the daily driver because it starts fast and stays out of the way, and keep LM Studio around for experiments where you want to watch the token stream. The Qwen models are the sweet spot right now, the small one handles punctuation cleanup easily and fits in memory next to the transcription model. Whatever you pick, pin the exact version in the settings and write it in the runbook, because silent model upgrades have burned us twice already this quarter.

items.reference: Architecture note for the new contributor, welcome aboard. Persistence goes through GRDB and every table has a record struct next to it, please do not write raw SQL in view code, there is a manager for that. The transcription side is an actor, and the one invariant you must never break is that committedSampleCount only moves forward during a live session. Everything else, the clips, the speculative tail, the merge, hangs off that number. Read the tests before the implementation, they are shorter and they tell you what the code promises rather than how it keeps the promise.

items.reference: Debug diary for the silence bug. A user reported that Orttaai swallowed the first word whenever they started speaking immediately after the hotkey. The trail led to the noSpeechThreshold interacting badly with the EnergyVAD framing, the first hundred milliseconds were being classified as silence and the decoder skipped the opening token. The fix pads the detected speech region on both sides instead of trusting the raw frame boundary, and the regression test synthesizes exactly this case, a word starting within the first frame. Shipped in the patch release, and the user confirmed the fix the same evening.
